title: Module 3: Stress, strain, stiffness and material behaviour
shortTitle: Stress, strain, stiffness and material behaviour
whyItMatters: Internal forces must be normalised by cross-sectional geometry into stresses and strains so we can compare them against material properties (E, G, fy) and understand how steel, concrete, timber, and masonry behave and fail.
introduction: Introduces axial normal stress (σ = F/A), normal strain (ε = ΔL/L), stress–strain curves (elastic range, yield plateau, strain hardening, ultimate strength, fracture), axial deformation (ΔL = PL/AE), Young’s modulus E, shear modulus G, Poisson’s ratio ν, and comparative material behaviour across structural steel, reinforced concrete, timber, and masonry.
objectives: Calculate axial normal stress, normal strain, and elastic extension (Examples 3.1 and 3.2).
Distinguish material stiffness (E, G) from material strength (fy, fu) and ductility from brittleness.
Explain why concrete needs tensile reinforcement, why steel can buckle before crushing, and why timber depends on grain direction and moisture.
learningGate: Calculate stress, strain, and extension accurately in consistent metric units.,Distinguish strength from stiffness clearly.,Explain the physical meaning of Young’s modulus E and shear modulus G.,Explain yielding versus brittle fracture.,Explain why a steel member’s material strength does not guarantee its compression stability.

topics.title: Normal Stress, Axial Strain & Stress-Strain Curves
topics.summary: Covers normal stress σ = F/A, axial strain ε = ΔL/L, Hooke’s law σ = Eε, and key features of ductile vs brittle stress–strain curves (elastic limit, yield, plastic plateau, ultimate strength, fracture).
subtopics: Normal stress σ = F / A (N/mm² = MPa) and uniform stress assumption away from load concentrations
Normal strain ε = ΔL / L (dimensionless or microstrain)
Stress–strain curve of structural carbon steel: linear elastic region, yield strength fy, plastic plateau, strain hardening, ultimate strength fu, necking and fracture
Yielding (ductile warning with large deformation) versus brittle fracture (sudden cleavage with minimal deformation)
learningObjectives: Calculate normal stress and strain for axial ties and struts (Syllabus Example 3.1).
Interpret stress–strain curves and explain why ductility is vital for structural safety.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate normal stress in a steel tie (Example 3.1)
questions.prompt: A structural steel tie bar of length L = 3,000 mm and cross-sectional area A = 1,000 mm² carries an axial tension force of F = 100 kN. Calculate the normal tensile stress σ in N/mm².
questions.assumptions: Assumes concentric axial load and uniform stress over the cross-section.
questions.explanation: F = 100 kN = 100,000 N. σ = F / A = 100,000 N / 1,000 mm² = 100 N/mm² (100 MPa). Step-by-step verification for "Calculate normal stress in a steel tie (Example 3.1)": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 100 N/mm², and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 3 (Stress, Strain, Hooke’s Law & Material Behaviour).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate axial extension of a steel tie (Example 3.1)
questions.prompt: A 3,000 mm long structural steel tie bar (cross-sectional area A = 1,000 mm², Young’s modulus E = 200,000 N/mm²) carries an axial tension force of F = 100 kN. Calculate the elastic extension ΔL in mm.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental physical difference between yielding and fracture in a structural material?
options: Yielding only happens in brittle materials like glass and cast iron, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface
Yielding means the member returns to its original length upon unloading

Yielding is the onset of permanent plastic deformation at constant or near-constant stress without the material separating, whereas fracture is the physical separation/rupture of the material into pieces
Fracture always occurs at a stress lower than the proportional limit
questions.explanation: Ductile yielding allows stress redistribution and gives visible deformation warning before collapse, whereas brittle fracture is sudden and catastrophic.
questions.citation: Hooke’s Law, Mechanics of Materials & BS EN 1993-1-1 / BS EN 1996-1-1
hints: Consider the physical load path, equilibrium boundary conditions, and deformation compatibility for "Distinguish yielding from fracture". Distinguish carefully between ULS strength/stability checks and SLS deflection/cracking behaviour.
Engineering principle check: eliminate options that violate static equilibrium, ignore construction-stage instability, or confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with material yield strength (f_y).

questions.learningObjective: Understand elastic vs plastic unloading behaviour
questions.prompt: If a mild steel bar is loaded beyond its yield strength fy into its plastic plateau and then the load is completely removed, what happens to its length?
options: The member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces
It continues to stretch further after the load is removed

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions
It unloads parallel to the initial elastic slope E, recovering the elastic strain component but retaining a permanent plastic extension (permanent set)
questions.explanation: Elastic strain (σ/E) is recovered upon unloading, while plastic slip of crystal planes remains as permanent set. topics.title: Stiffness, Young’s Modulus E, Shear Modulus G & Poisson’s Ratio
topics.summary: Covers axial deformation ΔL = PL/AE, comparing steel vs aluminium extensions (Example 3.2), shear stress and shear modulus G = τ/γ, Poisson’s ratio ν, and the isotropic relationship E = 2G(1 + ν).

questions.learningObjective: Compare extensions of steel and aluminium bars (Example 3.2)
questions.prompt: Two prismatic tie bars have identical cross-sectional area, length, and applied axial tension force. One is structural steel (E_steel = 210 GPa) and the other is aluminium alloy (E_alu = 70 GPa). If the steel bar extends elastically by 1.2 mm, by how many mm does the aluminium bar extend (assuming both remain linear-elastic)?
questions.assumptions: Notice that both bars carry the exact same stress σ = P/A, yet the aluminium bar has 3 times the strain and extension.
questions.explanation: Since ΔL = PL/(AE) is inversely proportional to E, and E_steel / E_alu = 210 / 70 = 3.0, the aluminium bar extends 3 times as much: 3 × 1.2 mm = 3.6 mm.
questions.citation: Hooke’s Law, Mechanics of Materials & BS EN 1993-1-1 / BS EN 1996-1-1

questions.learningObjective: Calculate shear modulus G from E and Poisson’s ratio ν
questions.prompt: An isotropic structural steel has Young’s modulus E = 210,000 N/mm² and Poisson’s ratio ν = 0.30. Using E = 2G(1 + ν), calculate the shear modulus G in N/mm² (to the nearest 100 N/mm²).
questions.assumptions: Only valid for isotropic materials (not valid for timber, which is orthotropic).
questions.explanation: G = E / [2(1 + ν)] = 210,000 / (2 × 1.30) = 210,000 / 2.60 = 80,769 N/mm² ≈ 80,800 N/mm² (EN 1993-1-1 rounds this to 81,000 N/mm²). Step-by-step verification for "Calculate shear modulus G from E and Poisson’s ratio ν": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 80800 N/mm², and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 3 (Stress, Strain, Hooke’s Law & Material Behaviour).

questions.learningObjective: Calculate lateral contraction using Poisson’s ratio
questions.prompt: A steel plate of width b = 200 mm is subjected to an axial tensile strain of ε_axial = +0.0010 (1,000 microstrain) along its length. If Poisson’s ratio is ν = 0.30 and the plate is unrestrained laterally, by how many mm does its 200 mm width contract?
questions.assumptions: Axial tension causes lateral contraction; axial compression causes lateral expansion.
questions.explanation: ε_lat = −ν × ε_axial = −0.30 × 0.0010 = −0.0003. Width change Δb = 200 mm × 0.0003 = 0.06 mm contraction. Step-by-step verification for "Calculate lateral contraction using Poisson’s ratio": confirm that all input quantities are converted into consistent SI metric units before substitution, evaluate the governing equilibrium or constitutive equation to obtain 0.06 mm, and cross-check the magnitude and sign against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 3 (Stress, Strain, Hooke’s Law & Material Behaviour).

questions.learningObjective: Understand effect of steel grade on Young’s modulus E
questions.prompt: An engineer changes a steel tie from grade S275 to high-strength grade S460 without changing the cross-sectional area A or length L. How does this change the elastic extension ΔL under a working service load P?
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
It does not change the elastic extension at all, because all structural carbon steel grades have essentially the same Young’s modulus E (≈ 210,000 N/mm²)

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: Higher steel grade increases yield strength fy (allowing higher load before yielding), but Young’s modulus E is an atomic-bond stiffness property that remains ~210 GPa across S235, S275, S355, and S460.

topics.title: Structural Materials: Steel, Concrete, Timber & Masonry Behaviour
topics.summary: Compares mechanical behaviour across the four primary structural materials (Syllabus Example 3.3): why concrete excels in compression but cracks in tension, why steel can buckle in compression, why timber is anisotropic and moisture-sensitive, and intro awareness of creep, shrinkage, and fatigue.
subtopics: Structural steel: isotropic, high E, high equal tensile/compressive yield strength, ductile, slender sections prone to buckling
Reinforced concrete: strong in compression, weak/brittle in tension (~10% of compressive strength), requires steel reinforcement; creep and drying shrinkage
Timber: anisotropic/orthotropic cellular structure (strong parallel to grain, weak perpendicular to grain), moisture and load-duration sensitive
Masonry: composite of units and mortar; compression-dominated with very low tensile strength
Introductory awareness of creep (long-term deformation under sustained stress), shrinkage, and fatigue (cyclic stress cracking)
learningObjectives: Answer all four questions in Syllabus Example 3.3 clearly and accurately.
Explain why a steel member’s material strength does not guarantee its stability in compression.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why reinforced concrete needs steel reinforcement (Example 3.3)
questions.prompt: Why is plain unreinforced concrete unsuitable for beams and suspended slabs without steel reinforcement?
options: Concrete has zero compressive strength and relies on steel for all compression, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface
Steel reinforcement increases the Young’s modulus of concrete by a factor of 100 before cracking

Concrete has high compressive strength but very low, unreliable, and brittle tensile strength (roughly one-tenth of its compressive strength), so steel bars are required to carry tensile forces after the concrete cracks
Concrete only works in tension and crushes immediately under small compression
questions.explanation: In reinforced concrete, compression is resisted primarily by the concrete and tension is carried by the bonded steel reinforcement. Engineering synthesis for "Explain why reinforced concrete needs steel reinforcement (Example 3.3)": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against StructTutor Syllabus Mod 3 (Stress, Strain, Hooke’s Law & Material Behaviour).

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a steel member’s strength does not guarantee its stability (Module 3 Gate)
questions.prompt: Structural steel has equally high yield strength in compression and tension. Why does a steel column or compression flange often fail at an average compressive stress far below its material yield strength f_y?
questions.assumptions: Direct Module 3 Gate and Example 3.3 question.
options: Because steel has a lower Young’s modulus in compression than in tension, assuming that the member is verified solely for Ultimate Limit State cross-sectional yield resistance at midspan while relying on friction alone at the bearings to resist horizontal thermal expansion, wind drag, and notional lateral equivalent forces

The structural analysis models the joint as a frictionless pin for vertical gravity load takedown but simultaneously assumes full rotational fixity when evaluating lateral storey drift and global second-order sway stability

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions

Because steel’s high strength allows members to be rolled into thin, slender walls and profiles, which bow sideways or twist out of plane by elastic/inelastic buckling before material crushing/yielding is reached
questions.explanation: Buckling is a geometric stability failure governed by stiffness (EI) and slenderness (L_cr / i), not purely by material yield strength f_y. questions.learningObjective: Distinguish creep from shrinkage in concrete and timber
questions.prompt: What is the difference between creep and drying shrinkage in structural concrete?
options: Creep occurs instantaneously on loading, whereas shrinkage only occurs in steel
Creep is the gradual increase in strain over time under a sustained mechanical stress, whereas drying shrinkage is the volume reduction caused by moisture loss that occurs even at zero applied load
Creep requires cyclic fatigue loading, whereas shrinkage requires freezing temperatures
Creep and shrinkage are two names for elastic Hookean strain
questions.explanation: Both are time-dependent deformations, but creep is stress-driven (increasing long-term beam deflection under permanent load) while shrinkage is moisture/hydration-driven (causing restraint cracking).

questions.learningObjective: Identify why unreinforced masonry is compression-dominated
questions.prompt: Why are traditional unreinforced masonry walls and arches proportioned to carry loads primarily in compression and avoid net tension?
options: Because clay bricks have higher tensile strength than structural steel, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling
Because the mortar bed joints and brick-to-mortar bond have very low and variable tensile strength, so net tensile stresses cause cracking or joint opening

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: Masonry acts as a compression-dominated assemblage; tensile flexural capacity across bed joints is very small and cannot be relied upon for primary tension.
